title: The Boastful Wife Who Claimed Great Virtue
summary: In the city of Basra lived a wealthy woman named Samira, who spent her days lecturing all the women of the neighborhood on the superiority of her morals, her absolute purity, an...
keywords: the whorish wife who vaunted her virtue
full_text:
In the city of Basra lived a wealthy woman named Samira, who spent her days lecturing all the women of the neighborhood on the superiority of her morals, her absolute purity, and her flawless character.
'None among you,' she would boast at every gathering, 'possesses my devotion, my discipline, and my spotless reputation. I am the very crown of virtue in Basra!'

Her husband, an honest merchant named Tariq, grew weary of her endless boasting, which alienated their neighbors and filled their home with cold vanity.
He resolved to test whether her supposed virtue was genuine or merely an empty cloak of pride.

One evening, Tariq arranged with an elderly, trustworthy kinswoman to visit their home disguised as a distressed widow seeking a night's shelter.
The old woman knocked at the door in threadbare clothes, shivering in the cold rain:
'I pray you, good folk, grant me a dry corner near your hearth for one night.'

Instead of showing the compassion she so loudly preached, Samira pushed the beggar away, scolding:
'Away from my gate! I do not allow ragged strangers near my clean rugs! It would tarnish the dignity of my household!'

Tariq intervened, brought the old woman inside, gave her warm broth, and let her rest in the guest chamber.
The next morning, the disguised kinswoman revealed her true identity before a gathering of the neighborhood elders.

Tariq spoke gently to his wife:
'Samira, thou hast spent years boasting of thy spotless virtue to the four winds. Yet when a cold, hungry traveler stood at thy door, thy virtue turned to stone.
True virtue does not consist in proclaiming oneself pure while despising the unfortunate; it lives in quiet kindness, humble service, and a heart open to those in need.'

Samira stood silent, her face burning with deep shame before her neighbors.
The lesson humbled her spirit: she ceased her self-righteous lecturing, opened her home to charitable works, and learned that the purest virtue is that which seeks no applause.
moral: True virtue is silent, modest, and proven by steady conduct, whereas loud boasting often conceals glaring flaws.
